passages.text: Molecular Mechanisms of Mouse Skin Tumor Promotion

Multiple molecular mechanisms are involved in the promotion of skin carcinogenesis. Induction of sustained proliferation and epidermal hyperplasia by direct activation of mitotic signaling pathways or indirectly in response to chronic wounding and/or inflammation, or due to a block in terminal differentiation or resistance to apoptosis is necessary to allow clonal expansion of initiated cells with DNA mutations to form skin tumors. The mitotic pathways include activation of epidermal growth factor receptor and Ras/Raf/mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling. Chronic inflammation results in inflammatory cell secretion of growth factors and cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor-alpha and interleukins, as well as production of reactive oxygen species, all of which can stimulate proliferation. Persistent activation of these pathways leads to tumor promotion.
1. Introduction

The development of cancer is a complex process during which a normal cell undergoes a progressive series of alterations resulting in the acquisition of an altered proliferative capacity, invasiveness and metastatic potential. These alterations are classically defined as occurring in stages: initiation involves DNA damage leading to mutation(s); this is followed by promotion, which involves enhanced proliferation and altered cell behavior; and finally progression results from subsequent genetic changes such as loss of heterozygosity and gene amplification. Classical tumor promoters are not mutagenic like carcinogens but rather cause an alteration of the expression of genes whose products are associated with hyperproliferation, tissue remodeling and inflammation. Ultraviolet (UV) radiation, on the other hand, is both mutagenic and tumor promoting and can therefore cause initiation as well as promote the clonal expansion of initiated cells.

The mouse skin model of multistage carcinogenesis (see Figure 1) has been extensively used to study molecular changes associated with the dysregulated signaling and altered gene expression relevant to the various stages of tumor development. Thus, this review on the mechanisms of tumor promotion focuses on this model system, although most of the principles are relevant to other epithelial tissues. The effects of different tumor promoters, as well as modulation of tumor promotion in various transgenic and knockout mice, in the skin model have illuminated the molecular mechanisms involved in promotion of tumorigenesis.
Multistage mouse skin carcinogenesis model.

Initiation occurs by exposure of the skin to either a chemical carcinogen or ultraviolet (UV) light, which causes a genetic mutation (either an activating mutation in a proto-oncogene such as H-ras or an inactivating mutation in a tumor suppressor gene such as p53) in the stem cell or progenitor cell compartment. Repeated exposure of the skin to chemical tumor promoters, UV light or other irritants including wounding promotes the clonal expansion of the initiated cell(s) as well as a generalized hyperplasia of the epidermis. Eventually initiated cells outgrow the normal epidermal cells to form premalignant papillomas. With further genetic changes, some of the papillomas convert to malignant carcinomas capable of invading through the basement membrane and finally metastasizing to the lymph nodes and lungs.

One of the cellular processes that is crucial for skin tumor promotion is the induction of cell proliferation and maintenance of a sustained hyperplasia. Initiated cells respond differently to repeated mitogenic stimuli and this allows their clonal expansion beyond that of the surrounding hyperplastic, but otherwise normal epidermis. Regenerative proliferation, such as that due to repeated wounding or ultraviolet (UV) light exposure, can promote tumorigenesis as well as chemicals and endogenous growth factors that induce cell proliferation. Alternatively, stimulation of cell signaling pathways that promote cell survival and/or inhibit apoptosis can be tumor promoting.

Another common feature of tumor promotion is induction of chronic inflammation. Tumor promoter-induced secretion of pro-inflammatory molecules by keratinocytes results in the recruitment of inflammatory cells, e.g., leukocytes, lymphocytes and macrophages, into the dermis. These activated cells then produce growth factors, cytokines and chemokines that promote cell proliferation, matrix remodeling, angiogenesis and suppression of adaptive immunity, all of which promote tumor growth. In addition, activated inflammatory cells produce reactive oxygen species (ROS) and nitric oxide resulting in oxidative stress, which has been shown to be associated with tumor promotion. For example, topical application of the contact allergen 2,4-dinitrofluorobenzene elicits a strong dermal inflammatory response and repeated treatments promote skin tumorigenesis.

ROS can also be produced in the target cells directly by tumor promoters. UVA wavelengths, which penetrate deeply into the skin, induce formation of ROS and oxidative stress in both epidermal keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts. The classical skin tumor promoter, 12-O-tetradecanoylphorbol-13-acetate (TPA), has been shown to increase production of ROS and hydroperoxides in keratinocytes both in vitro and in vivo and organic peroxides have been shown to promote skin tumorigenesis.

In general, the effects of tumor promoters are reversible for a limited number of applications; however, their prolonged epigenetic effects result in irreversible genetic events in the later stages of tumor promotion. So what are the molecular mechanisms by which tumor promoters cause changes in cell proliferation and gene expression? Tumor promoters, whether UV, chemicals or endogenous factors, usually interact at the cell's surface with specific receptors or other cell components that elicit several processes/responses, including enhanced DNA synthesis, increased production of eicosanoids, cytokines and growth factors, a pro-oxidant state and alterations in cell surface properties leading to changes in cell adhesion and cell-cell communication. Tumor promotion leads to altered gene expression and identification of these critical events offers targets for chemoprevention and/or therapy.
2. Receptors for Tumor Promoters
2.1. Protein Kinase C (PKC)

Early mouse skin carcinogenesis studies were performed using a low dose of a carcinogen, such as 7,12-dimethylbenz[a]anthracene (DMBA) or benzo[a]pyene (B[a]P), followed by repeated applications of an irritant such as croton oil (see e.g.,). Later, the active components of croton oil were identified as phorbol esters with TPA being the most potent. Finally, in the early 1980s, the receptor for phorbol esters was identified as PKC, which is a calcium-activated, phospholipid-dependent serine/threonine kinase. Diacylglycerol (DAG) is the endogenous ligand for PKC. DAG is generated along with inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate by cleavage of phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate by phospholipase C (PLC). Multiple isoforms of PKC have since been identified, some of which are not calcium- or DAG-activated. Several other non-phorbol ester classes of tumor promoters, despite apparent structural differences, have also been shown to bind to and activate PKC, including mezerein, teleocidins, lyngbyatoxin and aplysiatoxins.
2.1.1. Structure and Isozymes

Nine PKC isozymes have been identified and they are classified into three groups based on their structure and cofactor requirements. All of the isozymes have a N-terminal regulatory region containing a short pseudosubstrate domain that inhibits enzyme activity immediately preceding one or two cysteine-rich conserved C1 domains that form the phorbol ester/DAG binding site. A variable hinge region separates the regulatory region from the C-terminal catalytic region containing the C3 ATP-binding domain and C4 substrate-binding domain. The first discovered and best characterized group is the conventional or classical PKCs, which include PKCalpha, PKCbeta and PKCgamma. These isozymes also contain a C2 domain in the regulatory region that binds acidic lipids such as phosphatidylserine and calcium, which are required cofactors for their activity. The second group is the novel PKCs, which are calcium-independent and include PKCdelta, PKCepsilon, PKCeta and PKCtheta. The atypical PKCs, PKCzeta and PKClambda (human homolog is called PKCiota), contain only one C1 domain and are not activated by phorbol esters or DAG. PKCalpha, PKCbeta, PKCdelta, PKCepsilon, PKCzeta and PKCeta are the isoforms expressed in human and mouse skin.
2.1.2. Activation and Substrates

Newly synthesized PKCs associate with the membrane where they are phosphorylated in the activation loop of the catalytic domain by 3-phosphoinositide-dependent kinase-1 (PDK-1). This phosphorylation is essential for their catalytic activity and leads to autophosphorylation of two sites in the C1 and C2 domains, which releases the enzyme into the cytosol where it remains inactive though interaction of the pseudosubstrate domain with the substrate-binding domain. Upon displacement of the pseudosubstrate domain by ligands such as DAG, the enzyme becomes catalytically active. After activation, the PKC isozymes are translocated from the cytosol to specific subcellular membrane sites where they interact with specific receptors of activated C-kinases (RACKs). Membrane localization allows interaction with phosphatidylserine or other acidic lipid cofactors and greatly increases the affinity of conventional PKCs for calcium, both of which are needed for full activity. In addition, PKCdelta is uniquely activated by caspase-3 cleavage in the hinge region generating a soluble (rather than a membrane-associated) catalytically active fragment, which in turn can active pro-caspase-3, thereby amplifying apoptotic signaling.

DAG is rapidly metabolized and thus activates PKC only transiently, while TPA persists much longer and results in prolonged activation of PKC. However, sustained activation of conventional and novel PKCs leads to desensitization and down-regulation. Active PKC traffics to the endosomes via internalization of caveolae and is then sorted to a perinuclear compartment, where PKC is dephosphorylated rendering it inactive. However, for PKCdelta, phosphorylation is required for its subsequent degradation. PKC is then ubiquitinated and degraded via the proteasome pathway. So while TPA binding to PKC leads to its persistant activation, the prolonged activation also results in PKC down-regulation.

Numerous proteins have been identified as substrates for PKC (see for a list of 110 proteins). Only a few of the substrates and downstream signaling pathways relevant to tumor promotion will be mentioned here. PKC isoforms have been shown to activate the Ras/Raf/mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) cascade and to mediate growth factor-stimulated activation of MAPK/extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) and cell proliferation. Activation of this cascade by PKCs is complex and regulated at several levels. PKCalpha and PKCepsilon have been shown to directly phosphorylate and activate c-Raf-1. However, others have shown that targeting of c-Raf-1 to the membrane via Ras may be the mechanism by which PKCalpha and eta activates c-Raf-1, while phosphorylation by PKCalpha and betaI may be involved in the desensitization of c-Raf-1. In addition, conventional and atypical PKCs have been shown to phosphorylate Raf kinase inhibitory protein (RKIP) causing its dissociation from Raf-1 leading to activation of the downstream MAPK/ERK pathway.

Another MAPK, c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK), which is preferentially activated by cellular stress and inflammatory cytokines, has also been shown to be activated by phorbol esters and PKC. PKC phosphorylation of JNK at Ser129 requires RACK1 and augments JNK activation by its upstream kinases MKK4 and MKK7. Ultraviolet (UV) light, which can promote as well as initiate skin carcinogenesis, rapidly and potently activates JNK specifically via PKCdelta phosphorylation at Ser129.

The epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is directly phosphorylated by PKC on three threonine sites, in particular Thr654 in the cytoplasmic juxtamembrane region, and it was initially reported that this phosphorylation reduces EGFR tyrosine kinase activity. However, subsequent studies using mutant forms of EGFR have shown that neither phosphorylation at the PKC site Thr654 nor at a MAPK kinase (MEK) site Thr669 are sufficient for TPA/PKC inhibition of ligand-stimulated EGFR tyrosine kinase activity. It has since been demonstrated that while PKC phosphorylation of EGFR inhibits subsequent EGF-induced EGFR activation, pretreatment with EGF prevents the inhibitory effects of phorbol esters on EGFR signaling. This study also suggested that PKC-mediated juxtamembrane phosphorylation of EGFR and its related family member ErbB2 transiently amplifies EGFR signaling by enhancing the stability of liganded receptor oligomers, but this also enhances the internalization of the receptors. The latter effect explains the long-known phenomenon of loss of high affinity EGFR binding sites after TPA treatment or PKC phosphorylation of EGFR.

Additional PKC substrates that contribute to crosstalk with other signaling pathways include guanylate cyclase and adenylate cyclase with PKC phosphorylation resulting in enhanced activity for both. On the other hand, PKCalpha phosphorylation of the catalytic subunit of phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase (PI3K) decreases its lipid kinase activity. Since PI3K activity leads to PDK-1 activation and PDK-1 phosphorylates and activates PKC, this may represent a negative feedback loop to limit PI3K signaling. PKCzeta and PKCalpha activate the nuclear factor-kappaB (NF-kappaB) signaling pathway by phosphorylating and activating IkappaB kinase beta (IKKbeta), which in turn phosphorylates and targets for degradation IkappaB. However, at least in colon cancer cells, prolonged activation of PKC by TPA inhibits NF-kappaB signaling by disrupting the IKKgamma/heat shock protein 90 (Hsp90) complex leading to proteasome degradation of IKKgamma and subsequently IKKbeta.

Other recently identified substrates of PKCs include vimentin and RASSF1A. Phosphorylation of vimentin, an intermediate filament upregulated upon epithelial cell transformation, by PKCepsilon promotes integrin recycling and cell motility. RASSF1A (Ras association domain family 1A) is a tumor suppressor and is phosphorylated by PKC at Ser197 and Ser203 in the Ras association domain, which blocks its ability to reorganize the microtubule network allowing cell cycle progression.
2.1.3. Roles of PKCs in Tumor Promotion

Altered expression of PKC isozymes has been observed in a number of human cancers. While most studies report down-regulated expression of PKCalpha, beta and delta in human cancers, PKCepsilon has often been found to be overexpressed in various cancers relative to the normal tissue. Similarly for mouse skin carcinogenesis, transgenic and knockout mouse models have demonstrated distinct roles for different PKC isoforms.

PKCalpha is the major conventional PKC isoform in the epidermis and is highly expressed. Transgenic overexpression of PKCalpha in the basal layer of the skin via a keratin 5 (K5) promoter does not affect keratinocyte growth or differentiation, but a hyperinflammatory response results from a single application of TPA. The PKCalpha-induced inflammation is mediated by up-regulated keratinocyte expression of CXC chemokine receptor 2 (CXCR2) ligands, which recruit infiltrating neutrophils. Although overexpression of PKCalpha does not affect skin tumorigenesis in the standard DMBA/TPA protocol, when a low dose of TPA is used, tumor development and conversion to carcinomas is greatly enhanced in K5.PKCalpha transgenic mice. On the other hand, PKCalpha null mice have increased susceptibility to skin carcinogenesis even though TPA-induced epidermal hyperplasia is reduced. Thus, PKCalpha appears to be important for TPA induction of proliferation and inflammation, but it has contradictory roles in skin tumor promotion.

PKCdelta is expressed in the basal cells of the epidermis and it contributes to the early onset of differentiation and keratinocyte apoptosis. Transgenic mice that overexpress PKCdelta in the basal layer via a keratin 14 (K14) promoter are resistant to standard two-stage skin tumorigenesis in that they develop significantly fewer number of papillomas and carcinomas. Suppression of TPA tumor promotion by PKCdelta overexpression results from enhanced TPA-induced apoptosis and inhibition of TPA-induced proliferation. On the other hand, UV induction of skin tumors, apoptosis and epidermal proliferation are similar in K14.PKCdelta transgenic mice as in wild-type mice. While transgenic overexpression of PKCdelta has no effect on UV-induced apoptosis, retroviral transduction of a caspase-resistant mutant PKCdelta into human keratinocytes prevents apoptosis induced by UV. These data clearly demonstrate the pro-apoptotic function of PKCdelta activated by cleavage by caspase-3. Thus, although transgenic PKCdelta does not affect UV tumorigenesis, it counteracts TPA tumor promotion.

PKCeta is expressed primarily in the suprabasal granular layer of the epidermis and regulates cornified envelope formation. Cholesterol sulfate, which activates PKCeta, stimulates epidermal differentiation and suppresses skin carcinogenesis when applied before each tumor promoter treatment. PKCeta null mice show enhanced susceptibility to skin tumorigenesis, prolonged hyperplasia in response to TPA and delayed wound healing. Together, these results suggest that PKCeta inhibits tumor promotion through its regulation of epidermal differentiation and homeostasis.

PKCepsilon is expressed in basal keratinocytes and its activation leads to proliferation and modulation of integrin-mediated cell adhesion. K14.PKCepsilon transgenic mice are phenotypically normal at birth, but as the mice age they develop chronic inflammation, hyperproliferation and/or ulceration around the tail base, ears and eyes. Although these transgenic mice develop much fewer papillomas than wild-type mice in chemical and UV skin carcinogenesis protocols, more squamous cell carcinomas develop that appear de novo without going through a papilloma stage and that rapidly metastasize to regional lymph nodes. The level of PKCepsilon transgene expression correlates with epidermal expression of tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNFalpha) and both TPA and UV induce greater TNFalpha expression and release of TNFalpha into the serum in transgenic compared to wild-type mice. As described in more detail below, TNFalpha is a key tumor promotion cytokine that regulates many cellular responses including inflammation, immunity, cell proliferation, differentiation and apoptosis. Indeed, PKCepsilon transgenic mice are resistant to UV-induced caspase-8 activation and apoptosis. In addition, PKCepsilon overexpression enhances TPA- and UV-induced activation of signal transducer and activator of transcription-3 (Stat3) via direct interaction with and phosphorylation of Stat3 at Ser727. Stat3 activation has also been shown to be essential for skin tumor promotion. Thus, PKCepsilon promotes skin carcinogenesis via several mechanisms including among others, induction of TNFalpha and activation of Stat3.

passages.text: In summary, tumor promoter activation of several PKC isoforms, in particular PKCalpha and PKCepsilon, is critical for induction of proliferation and inflammation that is necessary for skin tumor development. Additionally, PKCepsilon-mediated changes in cell adhesion and motility enhance malignant progression. Conversely, down-regulation of other PKC isoforms, such as PKCdelta and PKCeta, also contributes to tumor promotion in the skin by attenuating epidermal differentiation and apoptosis.
2.2. Aryl Hydrocarbon Receptor (AhR)

The AhR, a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor, mediates the toxic and carcinogenic effects of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and halogenated PAHs. Unliganded AhR is sequestered in a cytoplasmic complex that includes Hsp90, hepatitis B virus X-associated protein 2 (XAP2), p23 and c-Src. Upon ligand binding, AhR is released from its chaperone complex, translocates to the nucleus and heterodimerizes with a related family member, aryl hydrocarbon nuclear translocator (Arnt). AhR/Arnt then recruits co-activators and/or co-repressors in the nucleus and binds to xenobiotic response elements (XREs) to regulate the transcription of target genes. The classical AhR target gene is cytochrome P450 CYP1A1, which is a member of the phase I monooxygenase enzyme superfamily that is involved in xenobiotic metabolism. Bilirubin, lipoxin A4 and the tryptophan derivative 6-formylindolo[3,2-b]carbazole (FICZ) have been proposed to be endogenous ligands for AhR. In some situations ligand-independent activation of AhR has been demonstrated. After ligand binding and nuclear translocation, AhR is rapidly degraded, which limits its signaling.

AhR is expressed in the skin and its xenobiotic ligand 2,3,7,8-tetrachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin (TCDD) can promote skin tumorigenesis in HRS/J hairless (hr/hr), although not in haired (hr/+) mice. PAH carcinogens bind to AhR and thereby induce cytochrome P450 enzymes, which are necessary for their metabolic activation. In complete skin carcinogenesis protocols, repeated applications of carcinogen induce tumor formation. Not surprisingly then, AhR null mice are completely resistant to B[a]P-induced complete skin carcinogenesis, as well as to B[a]P-induced subcutaneous tumorigenesis. Transgenic mice that overexpress a constitutively active form of AhR in the skin via a K14 promoter develop inflammatory skin lesions with up-regulated expression of multiple inflammatory cytokines in the epidermis. Recent reports have demonstrated that AhR plays a role in UV-induced responses in keratinocytes. Tryptophan absorption of UV irradiation leads to formation of FICZ, which is a high affinity ligand for AhR. This results in nuclear translocation of AhR and induction of CYP1A1 expression. At the same time c-Src is released from the AhR/Hsp90 complex and activates EGFR/MAPK leading to induction of cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2). UV induction of both CYP1A1 and COX-2 in the skin are completely blocked in AhR null mice.

Taken together, these data indicate that activation of AhR plays various roles in skin carcinogenesis by being the receptor for PAH carcinogens and inducing their activation, provoking inflammation in the skin and mediating some of the UV responses in the skin.
2.3. Peroxisome Proliferator-Activated Receptors (PPARs)

PPARs are in the nuclear hormone receptor superfamily and were identified in the 1990s as the receptors for peroxisome proliferators. PPARs form heterodimers with another superfamily member, the retinoid receptor RXR, and bind to peroxisome proliferator response elements (PPREs) in the promoters of target genes. Three PPAR isoforms encoded by separate genes are differentially expressed: PPARalpha is expressed in the liver, kidney, intestine, heart, skeletal muscle, brown adipose tissue, adrenal gland, skin and pancreas; PPARbeta (also called PPARdelta) is ubiquitously expressed; and PPARgamma is expressed primarily in adipose tissues and to a lesser extent in the intestine, retina, skeletal muscle and lymphoid tissues.

Endogenous ligands for PPARs include fatty acids and COX- and lipoxygenase (LOX)-generated eicosanoids. Long chain (C16-20) polyunsaturated fatty acids (e.g., linoleic, arachidonic and docosahexaenoic acids) bind to and activate all three isoforms of PPAR. In a more isoform-specific manner, certain arachidonic acid metabolites are also effective ligands for the PPARs. Of LOX products, 8S-hydroxyeisocatetraenoic acid (8S-HETE), is a specific activator of PPARalpha, while 15S-HETE activates PPARgamma. Prostaglandins (PGs) derived from COX metabolism of arachidonic acid, PGA1 and PGD2, activate PPARbeta/delta, while PGD1, PGD2 and 15-deoxy- 12,14-PGJ2 activate PPARgamma. Thus, PPARs maintain lipid homeostasis by acting as sensors of fatty acid and lipid levels and then inducing the expression of fatty acid metabolizing enzymes.

In the skin tumorigenesis model, PPARalpha ligands conjugated linoleic acid and Wy-14,463 moderately inhibit TPA tumor promotion. PPARalpha is found in the epidermis as well as in skin papillomas and carcinomas and is most highly expressed in cultured keratinocytes that have been induced to differentiate by high calcium levels. The endogenous PPARalpha ligand 8S-HETE, which is produced by 8S-LOX after skin irritation, induces keratinocyte differentiation and PPARalpha-mediated transcription. Like exogenous treatment with PPARalpha ligands, overexpression of 8S-LOX in the epidermis via a loricrin promoter, which results in elevated 8S-HETE levels, inhibits two-stage skin tumorigenesis. Thus, in the skin, activation of PPARalpha inhibits tumor promotion.

The inflammatory cytokine, TNFalpha, induces PPARbeta/delta expression in epidermal kertinocytes. Cytokine-induced activation of PPARbeta/delta enhances cell survival by up-regulating antiapoptotic and down-regulating proapoptotic genes, but also induces cell cycle arrest and terminal differentiation of keratinocytes. Thus, PPARbeta/delta may have either pro- or anti-tumorigenic activities depending on the context.
3. Growth Factors and Receptors
3.1. Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR)/ErbB Family Signaling
3.1.1. Receptors and Ligands

Epidermal growth factor (EGF), acting through its receptor EGFR, is a potent mitogen for epidermal keratinocytes. Not surprisingly, since cell proliferation is necessary for tumor promotion, EGFR signaling plays an important role in skin carcinogenesis. Many human cancers, including lung, breast, brain, and ovarian cancers, also have dysregulated EGFR expression or activity due to gene amplification, mutations or overexpression of ligands.

passages.text: EGFR (or ErbB1) is a member of the ErbB/HER family of transmembrane receptor tyrosine kinases, which also includes, ErbB2 (HER2 or Neu), ErbB3 and ErbB4. Ligands bind to the extracellular domain of EGFR, ErbB3 or ErbB4, which induces homodimerization and/or heterodimerization with ErbB2 and activation of the kinase domain in the cytoplasmic tail. Receptor dimerization results in autophosphorylation of key tyrosine residues within the cytoplasmic domain, which form docking sites for downstream adapter and signaling proteins, and subsequent tyrosine phosphorylation of the docked proteins. Adaptor/signaling protein recruitment and phosphorylation leads to activation of multiple signaling pathways including MAPK, PI3K/Akt and PLCgamma/PKC pathways (Figure 2). Cellular context, as well as the ligand bound and dimer composition leading to formation of specific docking sites on specific phosphorylated tyrosines determines which particular pathway(s) are activated. Signal transduction from the ErbBs leads to transcriptional activation of specific gene programs that affect cell proliferation, migration, differentiation, adhesion, and apoptosis.

The ErbB ligands are all characterized by a consensus sequence of six conserved cysteines that form three intramolecular disulfide bonds known as the EGF motif, which is necessary for binding to ErbB receptors. Ligands include EGF, transforming growth factor-alpha (TGFalpha), heparin-binding EGF-like growth factor (HB-EGF), amphiregulin, epiregulin, betacellulin and neuregulins (or heregulins). All ligands are synthesized as large transmembrane precursors that are released as mature growth factors by cell surface proteases. The ligands show preferential binding to different ErbB receptors such that EGF, TGFalpha and amphiregulin are specific for EGFR; HB-EGF, betacellulin and epiregulin bind to either EGFR or ErbB4; while the neuregulins bind to ErbB3 and ErbB4. ErbB2 has no known ligand, but heterodimerizes with the other ErbBs leading to potent and prolonged activation of downstream signaling pathways.

Growth factor signaling pathways important in tumor promotion. Epidermal growth factor (EGF) and other ligands of the EGF receptor (EGFR)/ErbB family of receptors, including transforming growth factor-alpha (TGFalpha), amphiregulin, heparin-binding EGF-like growth factor (HB-EGF) and betacellulin, activate signaling of both the Ras/Raf/mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) and extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) kinase (MEK)/ERK and phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase (PI3K)/Akt/mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathways. Insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) signals through its receptor IGF1R, which phosphorylates insulin receptor substrate-1 (IRS1) and SH2-containing protein (Shc) as well as other substrates leading to the activation of both Ras/Raf/MAPK and PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathways. Members of the transforming growth factor-beta (TGFbeta) family (TGFbeta1, TGFbeta2 and TGFbeta3) bind to TGFbeta receptor type II (TbetaRII) causing the recruitment of the type I receptor (TbetaRI), which phosphorylates Smad2 and Smad3 allowing them to form a complex with Smad4 that then translocates to the nucleus to modulate gene expression.
3.1.2. Role of EGFR/ErbB Signaling in Skin Tumorigenesis

The role of EGFR/ErbB signaling in mouse skin tumor promotion has been extensively studied. Single and multiple applications of various skin tumor promoters up-regulate epidermal expression of TGFalpha. TGFalpha expression is elevated in mouse skin tumors induced by DMBA initiation and promoted with either TPA or chrysarobin. Transgenic mice that overexpress TGFalpha in the skin via either a K14 or keratin 1 (K1) promoter develop papillomas upon wounding or with TPA treatment without carcinogen initiation, demonstrating that high expression levels of TGFalpha can act as an initiating event, as well as enhance tumor promotion. Conversely, wa-1 mice with a spontaneous inactivating mutation in the TGFalpha gene show only modest epidermal hyperplasia after multiple TPA treatments and are resistant to two-stage skin carcinogenesis. However, TPA induces the mRNA expression of other EGFR ligands, amphiregulin and HB-EGF, in wa-1 mice. TGFalpha null and wa-1 keratinocytes transformed with the v-H-ras oncogene and grafted onto nude mice give rise to skin tumors (mostly papillomas) similar to that of keratinocytes from BALB/c or C57BL mice (wild-type counterparts to wa-1 or TGFalpha null, respectively). The latter results suggest that TGFalpha is not necessary for v-H-ras induction of skin tumors and that other EGFR ligands may also contribute to tumorigenesis.

Early studies showed that various skin tumor promoters including TPA, chrysarobin, thapsigargin, palytoxin and UVB irradiation, as well as TCDD inhibit the ability of EGF to bind to its receptor in short-term experiments in cultured cells (reviewed in). However, topical treatment in vivo with either TPA or chrysarobin significantly increases EGF binding to EGFR in the long term. Multiple applications of TPA, chrysarobin or okadaic acid result in increased tyrosine phosphorylation (activation) of EGFR and elevated levels of activated EGFR are found in skin papillomas. Similarly, UV exposure rapidly activates EGFR. Tyrosine kinase inhibitors, which block EGFR signaling, are able to inhibit TPA-induced epidermal hyperplasia and cell proliferation. UV-induced epidermal hyperplasia is completely abrogated in EGFR null mice, while UV-induced apoptosis is enhanced. Grafts of EGFR-null keratinocytes transformed with v-H-ras yield skin tumors that are much smaller than wild-type keratinocytes, which demonstrates that EGFR signaling contributes to tumor growth. EGFR-null keratinocytes immortalized with human papilloma virus (HPV)-16 are unable to form tumors when grafted onto nude mice, while HPV16-immortalized wild-type keratinocytes form tumors to some extent (17%), a few of which progress to carcinomas. Taken together, these results demonstrate that EGFR signaling is important for keratinocyte proliferation, survival and skin tumor promotion.

In addition to EGFR, ErbB2 and ErbB3 are expressed in mouse keratinocytes in culture and in mouse epidermis in vivo. TPA treatment results in increased tyrosine-phosphorylated ErbB2 and formation of EGFR:ErbB2 heterodimers in the epidermis. Similarly, K14.TGFalpha transgenic mice show activation of ErbB2 in the skin. K5.ErbB2 transgenic mice display both follicular and epidemal hyperplasia and develop spontaneous skin tumors, some of which progress to squamous cell carcinomas. The epidermis of these mice has elevated levels of EGFR as well as ErbB2, shows EGFR:ErbB2 and ErbB2:ErbB3 heterodimer formation and tyrosine phosphorylation. ErbB2 transgenic mice are more sensitive to TPA-induced epidermal proliferation and two-stage skin tumorigenesis compared to wild-type mice. Thus, ErbB2 signaling via heterodimerization with EGFR and/or ErbB3 strongly enhances epidermal growth and skin tumorigenesis.
3.2. Insulin-like Growth Factor-1 (IGF-1) and Receptor

IGF-1 and IGF-2 are single-chain polypeptides that structurally resemble proinsulin and both have mitogenic activity. Expression of IGF-1 is regulated primarily by pituitary-derived growth hormone and its expression and secretion by the liver is responsible for the majority of circulating levels. Both IGF-1 and IGF-2 bind to and signal through the IGF-1 receptor (IGF-1R), which is a receptor tyrosine kinase consisting of an extracellular alpha subunit homodimer and a transmembrane beta subunit homodimer. IGF-1 binding to the extracellular alpha subunits activates the cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase domains in the beta subunits resulting in autophosphorylation on tyrosine residues, which allows docking and phosphorylation of its major substrates, insulin receptor substrate-1 (IRS-1), IRS-2 and Shc. IGF-1R signaling leads to the activation of the PI3K/Akt pathway through phospho-IRS-1 or the activation of the Ras-Raf-MAPK pathway either through phospho-IRS-1 or phospho-Shc (Figure 2). IGF-1/IGF-1R signaling results in stimulation of cell proliferation and/or cell survival/inhibition of apoptosis.

IGF-1/IGF-1R signaling has been implicated in the promotion of carcinogenesis in both humans and animals (reviewed in). In the mouse skin model, IGF-1 mRNA levels are elevated consistently in papillomas and carcinomas, while IGF-1R mRNA is up-regulated in some but not all tumors, mostly carcinomas. Unlike TGF-alpha, single or repeated applications of the tumor promoter TPA fails to alter IGF-1 expression. Transgenic mice that overexpress IGF-1 in the epidermis via either a K1 or K5 promoter are hypersensitive to the proliferative effects of TPA and develop skin tumors without carcinogen initiation. Using of the two-stage protocol with DMBA plus various tumor promoters, the K1.IGF-1 transgenic mice develop more tumors/mouse more rapidly than their non-transgenic littermates. K5.IGF-1 transgenic mice also form skin tumors with only DMBA initiation. Together these data demonstrate that IGF-1 overexpression contributes to both initiation and promotion of skin tumorigenesis. On the other hand, liver-specific IGF-1 deficient (LID) mice, which have ~75% reduction in circulating IGF-1 levels, have a reduced response to two-stage skin carcinogenesis and less activation of both IGF-1R and EGFR in response to TPA compared to wild-type mice. Thus, circulating IGF-1 also contributes to skin carcinogenesis.
3.3. Transforming Growth Factor-beta (TGFbeta) and Receptors
3.3.1. TGFbeta Signaling

The TGFbeta family includes three members, TGFbeta1, TGFbeta2 and TGFbeta3. All three TGFbetas are secreted as latent complexes, which consist of dimers of their C-terminal mature peptide and N-terminal pro domain in association with a latent TGFbeta-binding protein that targets and sequesters TGFbeta in the extracellular matrix. TGFbeta must be released from the matrix and activated by proteolysis or conformational change in order to bind to and signal through its receptors. Active TGFbeta initially binds to homodimeric TGFbeta type II receptor (TbetaRII), which results in recruitment of a dimer of type I receptor (predominantly TbetaRI, also called ALK5) to form a heteromeric complex. The TbetaRII cytoplasmic serine/threonine kinase domain phosphorylates the GS domain of TbetaRI, which results in activation its kinase domain and autophosphorylation, as well as phosphorylation of downstream targets, in particular Smad2 and Smad3. Phosphorylated Smad2/3 is then able to form a complex with Smad4, which then translocates to the nucleus, where the Smads directly and indirectly regulate gene transcription (Figure 2).
3.3.2. Multiple Roles of TGFbeta Signaling in Tumor Promotion

The role of TGFbeta signaling in cancer and tumor promotion is multifaceted and complex. TGFbeta is growth inhibitory to epithelial cells and induces apoptosis in several cell types and so acts as a tumor suppressor. Growth inhibition by TGFbeta is due to repression of c-myc transcription via a Smad3/4, E2F4/5 and p107 complex forming on its promoter, and to up-regulation of the transcription of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors p15ink4b and p21cip1 via interactions between Smads and Sp1 on their promoters. Malignant progression is often associated with development of resistance to the growth inhibitory effects of TGFbeta, and a number of different human cancers have inactivating mutations in genes for TGFbeta receptors, Smad2 or Smad 4. On the other hand, many cancers overexpress TGFbeta1 and TGFbeta signaling can promote carcinogenesis and cancer progression by inducing angiogenesis, cancer cell invasion into the extracellular matrix, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and metastasis, as well as by repressing immunosurveillance.

TGFbeta also has contradictory roles in inflammation and immune function. TGFbeta has anti-inflammatory actions since TGFbeta1 null mice develop multifocal inflammatory disease resulting in early death. However, TGFbeta1 is also a potent chemoattractant of neutrophils and transgenic mice that overexpress TGFbeta1 in the skin show inflammatory cell infiltration associated with up-regulated expression of proinflamatory cytokines and chemokines, such as interleukin-1 (IL-1), TNFalpha, interferon-gamma (IFNgamma), monocyte-chemotactic protein-2 (MCP-2) and others. Tumor-induced TGFbeta suppresses immune surveillance by inducing IL-17 expression in CD8+ T cells. Thus, although TGFbeta signaling can be anti-inflammatory and therefore tumor suppressive, its role as a chemoattractant and in immune suppression can contribute to promotion of tumorigenesis.
3.3.3. Role of TGFbeta Signaling in Skin Tumorigenesis

In the mouse skin model, TGFbeta1 mRNA is transiently induced in response to several different tumor promoters and is constitutively overexpressed in squamous cell carcinomas. However, loss of TGFbeta1 immunostaining in papillomas has been correlated with an increased risk of malignant conversion. Two-stage carcinogenesis experiments with transgenic mice that overexpress TGFbeta1 in the epidermis via either K6 or K10 promoters results in formation of fewer papillomas, but increased conversion to carcinomas and progression to aggressive spindle cell carcinomas with elevated TGFbeta3 expression. In an inducible transgenic model, induction of TGFbeta1 expression after papilloma development promotes progression to carcinomas that metastasize to lymph nodes. Transgenic overexpression of TGFbeta1 in papillomas is associated with up-regulated matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) expression, loss of membrane-associated E-cadherin/catenin complex and increased angiogenesis.

passages.text: Disruption of TGFbeta signaling by overexpression of a dominant negative TbetaRII in the epidermis via either K5 or loricrin promoters results in more skin tumor development in two-stage carcinogenesis protocols, with accelerated and greatly increased incidence of carcinoma development. Both premalignant and malignant tumors from these mice have increased angiogenesis along with elevated expression of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and reduced expression of thrombospondin-1. While TGFbeta1 transgenic mice develop spindle cell carcinomas demonstrating EMT, tumors from bigenic mice that overexpress both TGFbeta1 and dominant-negative TbetaRII do not, which demonstrates that TGFbeta signaling in the epithelial cells is required for EMT, while induction of invasion and metastasis is not. Together these results suggest that TGFbeta signaling is tumor suppressive at early stages via its growth inhibition of carcinogen-initiated epithelial cells; but as tumor cells become resistant to TGFbeta's growth inhibitory effects, TGFbeta produced by the tumor or other cells acts on the stroma to enhance malignant progression via induction of VEGF, MMPs and down-regulation of thrombospondin-1.

Smad null mice further demonstrate the opposing actions of TGFbeta signaling on tumor promotion in mouse skin. Smad3 null mice are resistant to TPA induction of epidermal proliferation and two-stage skin carcinogenesis with reduced infiltration of tumor-associated macrophages and expression of IL-1beta and MCP-1 in papillomas compared to wild-type mice. In contrast, mice with skin-specific knockout of Smad4 have epidermal hyperplasia and develop spontaneous malignant squamous cell carcinomas, which is associated with inactivation of phosphatase and tensin homolog deleted on chromosome 10 (PTEN), activation of Akt and nuclear accumulation of cyclin D1. Together these results suggest that Smad3 signaling is necessary for TGFbeta's proinflammatory effects, while Smad4 is important for TGFbeta's growth inhibitory and pro-apoptotic effects.
4. Proinflammatory Cytokines and Prostaglandins
4.1. Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha (TNFalpha)
4.1.1. Receptors and Signaling

TNFalpha is one of the critical cytokines mediating tumor promoter-induced inflammation. TNFalpha is synthesized as a type II transmembrane pro-peptide that forms a homotrimer and is released as a soluble factor upon cleavage by the metalloprotease TNFalpha-converting enzyme (TACE). TNFalpha signals through two homotrimeric transmembrane receptors, TNFR1 and TNFR2. TNFR1 is expressed constitutively in most tissues and preferentially binds soluble TNFalpha, while TNFR2 expression is restricted primarily to hematopoietic and immune cells and is activated only by membrane-bound TNFalpha. Ligand-bound TNFRs recruit multiple adaptor proteins that activate multiple signaling pathways. One adaptor protein is TNFR1-associated death domain protein (TRADD), which interacts with the cytoplasmic death domain of TNFR1 and serves to recruit binding of receptor-interacting protein kinase (RIP) and TNFR-associated factor-2 (TRAF2) to the receptor complex. On the other hand, TRAF2 homodimers or TRAF1/2 heterodimers bind directly to TNFR2 to activate downstream signaling. TNFalpha activation of TNFR1 initiates activation of NF-kappaB signaling by TRAF2 bound to TNFR1 via TRADD recruiting the IkappaB kinase (IKK) complex. Then RIP activation of the IKKs releases NF-kappaB from its inhibitory complex with IkappaB. TNFalpha stimulation of NF-kappaB transcriptional activity also occurs through PKCzeta and PI3K/Akt phosphorylation of the transactivation domain of the NF-kappaB p65/c-Rel subunit, as well as Akt phosphorylation of IKKalpha (Figure 3). NF-kappaB signaling leads to induction of a variety of antiapoptotic factors.

Another TNFR1-mediated signaling pathway is activation of the JNK cascade. TNFR1/TRADD/TRAF2 complex interacts with germinal center kinase (GCK) family members, which results in activation of the MAPK kinase kinases MKK7 and MKK4 upstream of JNK. In addition, TNFR1/TRAF2-dependent generation of ROS leads to activation of another MAPK kinase kinase, apoptosis signal-regulating kinase-1 (ASK1) that then associates with TRAF2 and phosphorylates MKK7. Finally, activated JNK phosphorylates the AP-1 transcription factor component, c-Jun, leading to transcriptional up-regulation of genes involved in proliferation, differentiation and apoptosis (both pro- and anti-apoptotic proteins).
Cytokine signaling pathways important in tumor promotion.

Tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNFalpha) binds to either of its receptors (TNFR1 and TNFR2), which recruit multiple adaptor proteins including TNFR1-associated death domain protein (TRADD), receptor-interacting protein kinase (RIP) and TNFR-associated factor-2 (TRAF2). Activation of TNFR1/TRADD signaling induces apoptosis through Fas-associated death domain protein (FADD) and caspase-8 and -10. On the other hand, TNFR1/TRADD/TRAF2/RIP causes activation of inhibitor of kappaB (IkappaB) kinase (IKK), which in turn phosphorylates and releases IkappaB from nuclear factor-kappaB (NF-kappaB) to activate NF-kappaB signaling. In addition TNFR1/TRADD/TRAF2 activates the MAPK kinase kinases 7 and 4 (MKK7 and MKK4)/c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK)/activator protein-1 (AP-1) signaling cascade either by interacting with germinal center kinase (GCK) or via generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and activation of apoptosis signal-regulating kinase-1 (ASK1). Interleukin-1alpha and beta (IL-1alpha and IL-1beta) bind to their receptor IL-1RI, which recruits IL-1R accessory protein (IL-1RAcP) and activates IL-1R-associated kinase (IRAK) that then activates the NF-kappaB signaling pathway. IL-12 and IL-23 are heterodimers with a common p40 subunit (green) disulfide-linked with either a p35 subunit (IL-12) or a p19 subunit (IL-23). IL-12 binds to its receptor consisting of IL-12Rbeta1 and IL-12Rbeta2, which associates with Janus kinase (JAK) family members JAK2 and TYK2 that then phosphorylate and activate signal tranducer and activator of transcription 4 (Stat4) leading to Th1 differentiation of T-helper cells. IL-23 binds to IL-12Rbeta1 coupled with IL-23R, which leads to JAK2 activation of Stat3 and Th17 differentiation of T-helper cells.
